title: Operators
description: Java's arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, unary, ternary, bitwise, and shift operators, and precedence.
objectives: Use arithmetic, relational, and logical operators
Understand unary, bitwise, and shift operators

content.heading: Arithmetic, Relational, and Logical Operators
content.body: Arithmetic operators are + - * / % (modulus), behaving like C's: integer / integer performs integer division. Relational operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) return boolean and, importantly, == on reference types compares object identity, not content — comparing two Strings' actual text requires .equals(), a very common Java gotcha covered in the Strings lesson. Logical operators are && (AND), || (OR), and ! (NOT), and are short-circuiting — the right-hand side of && or || is only evaluated if necessary, which is commonly relied on to guard against a NullPointerException (if (obj != null && obj.isValid())).

content.heading: Unary, Ternary, Bitwise, and Precedence
content.body:
Unary operators include ++ / -- (increment/decrement, either prefix ++x or postfix x++, which differ in whether the incremented value is used before or after the expression evaluates) and unary - / + for sign. The ternary conditional operator, condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse, is Java's compact if/else expression, usable inline. Bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~) and shift operators (<<, >>, >>>) operate on the binary representation of integer types — >>> is Java's unsigned right shift, filling with zeros regardless of sign, unlike >> which sign-extends.

Operator precedence in Java broadly follows the same order as most C-family languages: unary operators bind tightest, then multiplicative, additive, shift, relational, equality, bitwise AND/XOR/OR, logical AND, logical OR, ternary, then assignment (lowest). Parentheses always override precedence and are recommended whenever the order isn't immediately obvious.

content.explanation: The ternary operator gives a compact inline if/else. s1 == s2 compares references (different objects here), while .equals() correctly compares the actual text content.

keyPoints: % is the remainder/modulus operator; / on two ints performs integer division
== compares reference identity for objects (including String) — use .equals() for content equality
&& and || short-circuit, only evaluating the right side when needed
condition ? a : b is Java's ternary (inline conditional) expression
commonMistakes: Using == to compare String content instead of .equals()
Confusing prefix ++x and postfix x++ semantics in a larger expression
Forgetting integer division truncates when dividing two ints
